Jonas / Ben / Lauren — internal note before we reply externally.

Engineering (Ben) helped draft the following points based on current metering rules for hosted API (we should validate with billing legal, but this is accurate operationally):

- Metering unit: For hosted text generation we bill on tokens consumed by the request as processed by the serving runtime. That includes prompt tokens that are sent to the runtime and tokens generated.

- Prefix cache (exact-match KV) behavior: if a request can be satisfied from an existing in-memory KV cache (same model, same prompt hash, compatible model variant) then the runtime avoids re-executing the attention passes. In practice, we consider a cache "hit" any time the KV lookup returns the necessary keys for the requested prefix without re-computation.

- Billing for cache hits: We do not bill for the CPU/GPU operations saved by a hit; however, billing still attributes the original prompt token volume to the request unless the call is explicitly using our "prefetch/warm-cache credit" mechanism. Put simply: cache hits reduce client latency and runtime compute, but unless the call is marked as a cache-prefetch or a background warm operation (which is eligible for pre-negotiated credits), the tokens for the prompt are considered part of the billed token count.

- Cross-session hits: Cross-session reuse is allowed (multi-tenant warm hits) as long as the prompt fingerprint and model match. But from a metering perspective it looks the same as any other request — token attribution happens at request time. Only requests explicitly flagged as "warm-prefetch" (background) and covered by a credit line are not billed for the prompt tokens.

- Practical example for Sofia's flow: if the 1.5k system prompt is cached and a user session issues a call that re-uses the cached prefix and sends 400 new tokens, the hosted API will charge for the 400 new tokens plus the 1.5k prompt tokens unless the request was performed as a prefetch/warm operation under a credit line. If you use streaming with KV reuse inside a single session, the runtime can avoid re-sending the prompt in subsequent turns; those subsequent turns will not be charged the full prompt again because the request payload is smaller.

- TTL/expiration: caches are opportunistic; hits are not guaranteed for a given time window. We recommend explicit warm-prefetch for high-assurance scenarios (see SOW appendix).

Short technical clarifications to Marissa's summary:

- "Prefetch/warm-cache credit" is a negotiated commercial item. When customers want deterministic warm state across millions of sessions we typically propose a small background prefetch job that builds the KV state proactively and we provide credits (or carve that into the commit) since it doesn't correspond to a synchronous user request.

- Cache hit vs request payload: if the request payload omits the 1.5k (because client reuses a session-level state), billing reflects what is sent. If the client still sends the prompt text in the request payload, it's billed even if the runtime short-circuits the compute.

- Suggested language for external: "Cache hits reduce compute but do not automatically change token metering unless you use our documented warm-prefetch credit approach; we can include prefetch credits in an annual commit."

If agreed, I'll attach the Q2 rate card and a sample commercial paragraph for the SOW.

Hi Sofia — apologies for the wall of text; here's the concise answer you can share with procurement and the three attachments I promised (rate card + example trace + SOW draft). If you want, we can redline the SOW with your procurement team.

Short answer (what is billed):
- By default, hosted API metering attributes token volume to the request payload at request time. That means if a request includes the 1.5k-system prompt in the payload, the tokens are billed even if the runtime served much of the work from a cached KV.

When cache hits reduce billing:
- Background warm-prefetch jobs and explicitly flagged prefetch requests are eligible for pre-negotiated credits (we can include these credits in your commit). These are typically used to warm the model state at scale so that subsequent synchronous user calls are low-latency — the prefetch operations themselves are not billed per-token if covered by credits in the commercial.

Cross-session reuse and multi-tenant flows:
- Cross-session prefix hits are supported but are treated the same for metering: billed at request time unless you route warming through the prefetch credit mechanism. There is no automatic "free cross-session hit" policy.

Practical recommendations for Nimbus Retail:
1) Short pilot: 30-90 day pilot with a 50k/month commit so we can measure cache-hit rates in your traffic pattern. We can give a pilot-level credit allocation to cover background prefetching for the shared system prompt.
2) Commit tiers: standard hosted tiers are in the attached rate card — as a datapoint, 10–25% discounts are typical at annual commit scale in the mid six-figure band; we can propose a tailored tier once we have usage forecasts.
3) SOW language: see NR-SOW-draft.docx (appended) for prefetch credit wording and acceptance criteria for warm-state success.
